utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Do you hear me? First of all, we would like to thank you for having come. We're going to ask you to rise, but you are being covered by protective measures; therefore, you're going to stand but just for a very short time, just as long as it takes to identify your name. We hope there are no mistakes in the spelling of your name. First identify yourself but don't say your name. That is, in fact, your name. Now you're going to take an oath, according to a statement which is going to be read to you and which you are going to repeat. Please repeat after the registrar. Read it slowly, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: If you would please repeat after me: I solemnly declare.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That I will speak the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That I will speak the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The whole truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The whole truth.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well, Witness DQ, that is what we're going to call you, please be seated. This is a public session, but there are many things that should not be in public. Defence counsel or the Prosecution will ask us to ensure that those details are not revealed. You have nothing to fear. You are in front of Judges. You have agreed to come, and we thank you for having done so. You are now going to testify. First you will answer the Defence counsel's questions, that is, the counsel for General Blaskic who is in this courtroom. You can speak in a very relaxed fashion. Do not be afraid. If you are tired, if you have any problems, please do not hesitate to tell us and we will take a break. All right, Mr. Nobilo, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, excuse me, unfortunately, it's a repetition of what happened yesterday, so if we could go into closed session for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. We'll go into a private session, a private session for a few moments in order to settle the complicated issues that arise before this Tribunal, which seem to be like no other issues. Let me say this for the public which is here in great numbers today. I would like to say good morning to the public as well and to remind the public that these are always open sessions, unless there are secrets which have to be kept from the public, but I consider it very important that the hearings be open as much as possible. (Private session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Open session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Then we will go back into a private session. But I would like to explain things. We must render clear and transparent justice for the public, and I would like things to be clear in respect of those who are listening to us and to the greater public, for example, on the internet. We are sitting pursuant to a Rule in our Rules of Procedure and Evidence which allows us to sit as presiding officers, that is, we remain Judges, but in order to make up for any problems that are caused by the sudden illness of one of our colleagues who is not here today, in agreement with the Defence and the Prosecution and, of course, with the accused, we could continue to hear the depositions as if they were being presented before presiding officers, and then the absent Judge will be informed of everything that was said, and if necessary, the witness can be asked to come back so that further questions can be asked. That's an explanation which explains why we can continue to sit and an explanation which explains why we are not in our robes today. Second point: The Tribunal has difficulty in collecting evidence, and those of you who have been listening to us yesterday understand these problems, we should not say it's this one's fault or that one's fault, but this is a problem of international justice in respect of crimes which were allegedly committed in a far away territory in which it is difficult to gather evidence and which leads to these problems which might appear trivial to you, that is, spelling problems, but they are important because the parties cannot assume their responsibilities, that is, conduct their cross-examinations, and we have to try to make up for this kind of problem, as well as others. Therefore, despite the delay that this has caused, we can begin with Witness DQ. Perhaps for a few moments, we're going to go back into a private session only to cover the identifying elements, and after that, we will go back into public session. Is that what you're asking, Mr. Nobilo?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. Just a few moments in order to clarify some of the identifying elements for the Judges. Thank you very much. (Private session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Open session)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness DQ, we shall immediately move on to the events of the 18th of September, 1993. Tell me, where were you on the morning of the 18th of September, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I spent all week at the hospital. This hospital was in our church. My husband was there, he was wounded, and I spent all of that week with him. On Saturday, the 18th of September, I went home --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you were in the hospital and that the hospital was in the church?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please describe to the Court what this hospital looked like?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is really pews that were put together, and then there were sponges between, and the heavily wounded men lay there, and they didn't really have much expert help. There weren't any doctors there to provide real medical treatment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you trying to say that inside the church, there was an improvised hospital, a make-shift hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was a hospital in the church.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Could we please view the first video clip and could we please have the lights dimmed?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please have a look at this and tell us, is that the church, the make-shift hospital where you nursed your husband? (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this the church in Nova Bila from the outside? Please, just press that button, yes. So is this the Nova Bila church from the outside?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't see a thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, can we start from the very outset because the witness has to see this first and foremost? Just a minute, please. We want to have the tape rewound, and then we're going to start from the beginning again. (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you see it now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this the church in Nova Bila?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, yes, this is where it was hit. A shell was damaged up there. These are our wounded. That's it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We're going to view the entire video clip, and then we're going to put questions to you. (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What we saw was the intensive care, the intensive care unit, and this is now within the church itself. The other thing we saw was -- well, not outside but it was apart from this. It was the room where the priests usually get dressed, and that is where the most heavily wounded men were, and that is where the intensive care unit was, and this is now within the church itself. These are the pews that were put together, and then sponges were put down, and this is where our wounded lay. You can see it here. See, these pews.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Croats did not have any other hospital in the Lasva Valley; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, this was the only hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. So this was a church hospital, so to speak, in Nova Bila, and your husband lay wounded there, and then you came to your village, we're not going to mention its name, so you came to your village on the morning of the 18th of September, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please describe to the court now what started happening then.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That morning, I came home to see what my child was doing, and I wanted to see what my old mother-in-law was doing too, and I wanted to prepare some food for them. I went out in order to get some potatoes to prepare lunch, but I never prepared that lunch. I started preparing breakfast. I put it on the table, and bullets started coming from all sides, and then shells, and I went out in order to put the cow in the barn because one had already been killed, and I wanted to have breakfast inside, but I didn't manage to have breakfast. I was hungry. We were all hungry. When the shooting got really bad, I tried to get out. First, my son went out. A bullet hit him and he fell, and I ran out after him, and I said, "Sonny, did anything happen to you," and he said, "No mother, I'm okay."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How old was your son then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Fourteen and a half. And then I went out, and since there was a lot of shooting, I still thought that the three of us could run away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the third person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My old mother-in-law. She was 73 years old. I was the first to leave, and the shooting resumed and I went back into the house. So I went into the bathroom because that was protected more than other parts of the house. So we stopped there, and an RPG grenade hit the upper story of my house, and we had no idea where to go, and I thought that the best shelter for us would be to hide where my pantry was, and I thought that we would be best protected there. So we walked in there and we closed the door, and we heard loud cries, "Allah-u-ekber. Kill the Ustashas." My son started to cry, and he said, "Mother, what are we going to do now?" And I said, "Son, we are going to wait." Then I heard the windows breaking from all sides, from the side that they were coming from. They got into the house. Some of them went upstairs, and some were shooting downstairs. All of a sudden, they went into the hallway and shot through the closed door, and they wounded my son. And he shouted and said, "Mother, I'm wounded. I can't stand anymore." And then I screamed, I opened the door, and I screamed at the top of my voice. I couldn't speak for another week. I'd lost my voice after that. And I saw two Arabs standing in my hallway, and my son tried to walk but then he fell, and an Arab took a knife and tried to cut my son's throat, and I grabbed his hands, and I begged him to slaughter me first and then my son.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before you proceed, could you please explain what these Arabs looked like? What kind of clothes did they wear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were short men. They had brownish clothes on and sneakers, and they had little beards. They were short, dark, dark, not too dark, and they spoke Arabic, they didn't speak our language at all, I mean, Bosnian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Two other Arabs came from the upper floor and one of them saw that my son was wounded. I don't know what he thought. They were saying something, of course I didn't understand anything, and this other one put his knife away, and then he started dragging my son across the hallway. And I was crying and I said, "Don't touch him, I'm going to carry my son." And my mother-in-law and I did carry him out. And they walked out after us, and he took the child from my arms and threw him onto the grass, and he fell. And he started getting up, he was on his elbows, and one of these men took a rifle and put it into the throat of my son. And I didn't understand anything he was saying except for "Ustasha, Ustasha," probably he was asking how many Ustashas there were. And I wanted to say something, and he hit me. And he probably said that he wasn't asking me anything, and he was pointing at my son and saying that he wanted to ask him something. I couldn't say a word. When I turned around to see whether any of my neighbours were around, underneath my house there were hundreds.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Hundreds of what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Hundreds of BH army men, and together with them were the Mujahedin. And he raised his hand, probably he wanted to ask what he was supposed to do with us. And I was looking down, and I thought that someone would help me. And he just waved away and probably said that he didn't want to kill us after all. I didn't understand a word of what they were saying. Then there was a wheelbarrow there, and they put my son on it and then they took us all to the Muslim village. When we got to the village, as I was on good terms with everybody, I didn't think they would do anything to me and that they would help me, that they would protect me from the Mujahedin. But when I came to the village nobody was there except for the army. I pleaded with them to protect me, but they separated me from my child, and they took my mother-in-law into one room and my child was taken out, somewhere outside. I cried and shouted, I didn't want to give them my child, and I shouted to them to give me back my child and I ran out like that, and I saw Jasko Dzelilovic running towards my child to kill him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (redacted) I pleaded with him, I said, "Jasko, the child has done nothing to you, please don't harm him, please protect my child, please." And he said that he would fuck my Ustasha mother and that he would slaughter us all. And they took me back to where I was before and I waited there for several instances, a Kombi van arrived, and (redacted). He was the worst bandit that ever lived. And he went in, took us away, took my son and started beating him and started breaking his leg. And you could hear the bones breaking, there was blood all over the place, there was bloodshed all over the place, and I pleaded with them. They told me to be quiet because they would kill me, too. And they kept threatening, "You will see what will happen to you when you come to the black house." That was the former camp which they inherited. And we went to, down there, and they started beating my child, and I screamed, and when I turned around I saw that my mother-in-law was lying on the ground (redacted) hit my mother-in-law, and she was on the ground. I tried to lift her up from the ground, but I did not succeed, because I could not see what was happening to the child. We kept turning around in circles. I appealed to everybody around me, but nobody would look at me. And then I saw (redacted), we were great friends, and I said, "(redacted), please help me, please help my child." But he turned away from me. "What do you want you Ustasha woman? How can I help you? We're not friends anymore."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one moment, please. All the names, I would like all the names struck from the transcript, but we can retain the phrase "Next door neighbour and best friend." Tell us, all your next door neighbours and that great friend of yours, were they all Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were, yes, they were all Muslims. For 30 years I had been living there and I never quarrelled with anybody, we never had any conflicts, any problems, we were always good friends and we would visit each other. When I turned around, I saw (redacted), he was a doctor, and he was one of my neighbours where I was born. And I pleaded him, I implored him, and that was the most difficult thing for me. I said. "(redacted), if you cannot save my child, give him something to make him die an easy death and not to have to go through this torture." And he said he would help me. And my child was lying on the sand naked, and (redacted), a doctor came up, and I asked him, because we were friends, "Please, (redacted), help my child. Please, please, take him away off the ground. You can see he is bleeding." And they lifted the child up from the concrete, they took him in there, they put a lingette on him. But I was crying, they sent me to the basement along with my mother-in-law, and I cried and screamed there, and they brought me my child. And I asked him "How are you, dear?" And he said, "Everything hurts, mother. Can you give me some water to drink?" And I said, "There is no water. There is nothing." He said, "Mommy, I'm hungry," and I said, "There is nothing, dear, we will just have to wait."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Try to calm down a little. If you would like a pause, if you would like us to take a break, I'm sure the Court will comply. All you have to do is ask. Tell us, your mother-in-law who was 73 years old, did they hit her, too?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I've already said that that man hit, my neighbour hit my mother-in-law, and she was lying on the ground.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened next? Your son was lying in the cellar, and you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, he was suffering great pain. I did not know what to do, I helped him as much as I could, as far as I was able. His leg went black and I had to loosen the bandages a little bit. But he said, "Mommy, I can't take this anymore." I tried call (redacted) because he was the main policeman, he was the main man in the police, he was above everybody else. And I said to him, "I know you are the head, I know that you can do everything, please help my child, call a doctor for him. He cannot go to the toilet." And that was the most difficult thing for him. And he said, "I'll see." I asked if we could go out to the toilet, just to see somebody who I might see to help me. And I saw (redacted) outside, and I pleaded with him, I implored him, I said, "(redacted), please, my child is in terrible pain. Can you save him?" And a little while later they came to the cellar, to the basement and put a catheter, they gave my son a catheter and helped him with his urinating problems. Later on they took me out for questioning. They asked me all kinds of questions which I couldn't answer. I did not know anything, I couldn't answer them. I wasn't interested in the war at all. And I was taken back to my child. I went back to my child, and in a little while later the Mujahedin arrived to question my child. And they made a cross and they said, "This is not Bosnia, this should not be present in Bosnia. In Bosnia everybody is going to be," and they made this sign across the throat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, we're having a transcript made here, so we have to describe what you have shown. You showed two twigs, and they made a cross out of these two twigs. And then you said -- yes, that's what I understood, because we didn't speak Bosnian properly. What did he describe to you then, could you describe it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He showed the sign of the cross made out of these two twigs, and he said, "We don't want this in Bosnia." That's what I understood him to say. Bosnia will be Muslim and everything that happens in Bosnia with a cross, it will no longer exist, that everybody would be slaughtered with this cross sign.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he indicated with his finger across your throat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he made a sign with the finger across my throat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We have to make some pauses in between what we're saying so that the interpreters have a chance to complete their interpretation. What happened next? Did another prisoner, an elderly man, come later on to your basement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I forgot to say that. About 4.00 on that same day when we were taken there, down the stairs they threw into the basement a man who was born in 1926 and that was (redacted). He was all black and blue and beaten up. And I asked him what had happened, and he said, "They beat me up." And I asked him, "How come you're here?" And he said, "Well, I'm here just like you're here." "How come they caught you?" And he said, "Well, I wanted to go back to the, from the forest to tend to my cows and they caught me and brought me here." "But why did they beat you up?" And he said, "I don't know. And they beat me up a great deal," and he was trembling. And I took an old dirty blanket and put it over him to stop him from shuddering. He shuddered a great deal, he shuddered all over, and he was beaten up. And that is what happened until nightfall. They came to get him again at nightfall and beat him up again, and once again, threw him back into the basement after they had beaten him up. And we were all huddled together in that basement. Another man who had, I suppose, been trench digging, he was wearing a prisoner's uniform, they all wore prisoner's uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say the first man, (redacted), is he a Croat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, he is. Yes, the second one is, was a Croat, too. His name was --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was his name perhaps (redacted)?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, his name was (redacted). And when he came I asked him, "How come you're here, (redacted)?" And he said, "I've been here from the beginning of the war. I don't count the days anymore, I count the months." And I said, "Where were you?" And he said, "I was taken to dig trenches, look at my hands." And his hands were all bloody.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So from the beginning of the war he was with the Bosnia-Herzegovina army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us move on now. It was the morning of the following day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on the morning my son, next morning my son was very ill. He had a temperature, he had a fever, he was extremely ill. (redacted) whether he had anything to give my child, some tea or anything that I could give him. But I wasn't thinking of myself, whether I was thirsty or hungry or whatever. And they said, "Well, fuck your mother, you can't have any food." But (redacted) came and brought my son some tea. It was salty tea, there was half salt and half tea, half sugar and half salt in the tea. And he said this is what had happened with the sugar, it had been mixed with salt. And my son said, "This is horrible to drink, mommy," and I said, "Never mind, son, drink it anyway. At least it is tea and it will refresh you a little bit." He was ill the entire time. And on the third day he was not able to take it anymore and he said, "Mommy, I'm dying, what can I do? Help me please." And I went out and banged on the door and (redacted) came. And I said, "(redacted) please, what do you want to do with my child? He can't take the pain anymore." And he said, "We'll see, perhaps you will not live anymore, perhaps you will be killed anyway the next day." And I said, "Well, I don't mind you can do it today, you can kill us today," because life was not important to me anymore. And they came a little while after, Dr. (redacted) came, and another doctor, I think his name was redacted), and they asked me what I wanted, and I said I wanted them to help my child. And they said, "We have to take him to hospital." "Where are you going to take him," I said. And my son said, "I would like to go(redacted) (redacted)" And they said, "Well, perhaps you will go there one day," said (redacted) to me, "but you are now going to be taken to Travnik." And a little while later, a van arrived and six armed Krajina soldiers turned up. And I wondered why they turned up, because my son was completely incapacitated. And they took him, he was naked, and they put him in the van, on the floor of the van. There was nothing there, it was bare. I rushed out after him, I was crying and screaming and shouting. I don't know what I was doing, I just lay, rolled in the dirt and the mud, and I couldn't leave my son and I couldn't send him away, either. Who was going to take care of him? They closed the van, I pleaded with them just to see my son a little while longer, and one of the men told me, I don't know him, one of these men from Krajina, they said, "Open the van, let this Ustasha woman see her son once again. We're going to slaughter him anyway up there, and we're going to throw him away. Does she think we're going to treat the Ustashas?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one moment please. On two occasions you mentioned the men from Krajina, who were these men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These were men that had fled there from Banja Luka, from Bihac, the Bihac area and Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were the Muslims expelled by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they came to Central Bosnia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they came to us in Central Bosnia, because they were promised that Central Bosnia would be cleared up of the Croats and that they would be able to live there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, perhaps we could take a break here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, we're going to take a break, the witness can rest up. Twenty-minute break. I just want to be sure that the names are taken out of the transcript. We will resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We can resume the hearing now. Have the accused brought in, please? (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Witness DQ, do you hear me? Have you been able to rest a little bit? Have you relaxed a little bit, if you can relax?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, a bit. Yes, I'm okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We're going to resume. We'll help you. If you have any problems, tell us and we can stop. Mr. Nobilo?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they took your son away to a hospital, to the hospital in Travnik in this Kombi, and that's where we stopped before the break. So could you please continue and tell the Court what happened afterwards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In this attack at our place, many people were killed. One man was caught alive, (redacted). They took him to the school, tortured him, and that's how they killed him. And when his body was exchanged, they could not recognise him at all. They just found on a very small part of his body a scar from an operation he had had before that. He was beyond recognition. Many people were killed then. (redacted). Two refugees from Jajce, redacted), they were underage. Then (redacted) was also killed, (redacted).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: (redacted)?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, (redacted).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please describe to the Court what happened to (redacted) born in 1920?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard that when these men from Krajina came, that they killed a man, they slaughtered him, and they cut off his ears, and they were waving his ears all over. He was an old man. He was born in 1920, and he was a sickly man too. So they had slit his throat. So these were terrible things, and then after that came my horror.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The fifth night of your stay there, when they all got drunk, they called for you; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First, when they took my son away, I cried all night, all night I cried. The door banged and somebody unlocked it. One of them came, one of them, and he put a torchlight in front of my face, the light was in my eyes, and I started screaming, I said, "Please don't. What do you want to do to me?" And he said, "What are you crying for? Get out." And I stood there, and he waited a bit, and he stayed there on his own, and then he said "Why are you crying?" And I said, "Is my son alive? I don't know anything about him." And he said -- he was (redacted). He said, "Don't cry. I'll help you. I'll go to Travnik and I'll bring you a letter from your son. You'll see that he's alive." And then I managed to compose myself a bit. I went back to the basement, and he told me to keep quiet and that I shouldn't tell anyone about this. On the fifth night, they all got drunk. I heard them screaming, I heard them playing music. One of them, (redacted), said, "(redacted) here," and I started crying, screaming. I woke up my mother-in-law, and I said, "Oh, what's going to happen to me now?" And some were shouting, "You shouldn't do that," and others wanted to. So there was some kind of a misunderstanding, they were quarrelling, and I was crying, crying, and everything went silent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you understand this, when you said that they wanted to take you out, what was your understanding of this? What did some people want to do and others had opposed this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I thought that they wanted to rape me. That's what I thought.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said a few minutes ago that many were killed when the BH army came into your village and hamlet. Tell me, did you notice any defence on the Croatian side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, and when I came down there, this friend of mine, former friend of mine, said to me, "Look at the Ustashas. They are all dispersed. No one is there. They didn't even fire a bullet." There were about 20 of our locals there who didn't even have rifles. There were a few rifles that were in the trenches, and then they all used the same rifle. Two soldiers would use the same rifle. And I said, "So many of you have attacked," and he said, "Yes, 800 headed by the Mujahedin," and I said, "Why?" And he said, "We want to join this place to the Mahala," and I said, "Why didn't you do it before that?" And he said, "We couldn't get the Mujahedin units in because we do not take any action without them," and that's it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the other civilians who did not escape? Where were they taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The other civilians who did not escape were all taken to this camp up there and were killed, whoever could not flee. So who stayed was killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At one point in time, did five Arab Mujahedin come and did they interrogate you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that was the night of the 9th -- I mean, I think a day before that a man came, a young man. They threw him into this cell, and they pretended to beat him a bit, and I asked him, "Who are you?" And he said, "I've been taken prisoner near Travnik, and they beat me," he said, and he didn't have any teeth, hardly any. Then he started asking us about this, that, and the other thing, and we said various things. And perhaps with all my troubles, I must have said something bad, something that they didn't like. And then they asked (redacted), "Old man, why did you go back? Why did you let them catch you," and he said, "I went to tend my cows and I thought that nothing would happen, and I thought that there was a bit of an attack and that they wouldn't come to our village," and that's how they caught him. And then they said to him, "Old man, that cow of yours is going to cost you your life," and all of a sudden we realised that he was not one of our people, that he was put in there to be amongst us. After that, five Mujahedin came to my basement, and (redacted) said to my mother-in-law, "Go out." They went out and I stayed there on my own. It was half dark in the basement. They brought me some kind of a map and they put it in front of my eyes, and they asked me where the trenches were, and I said, "Well, if our village has fallen, you probably know where the trenches are. How should I know?" "How many soldiers do you have? How many trenches do you have," they said, and I said, "It's only our locals. We haven't got anybody else. It's only us. We were the only ones there." And then they said to me, "Show us where the trenches are," and I said, "I can't see a thing. It's dark," and then they said, "You Ustasha motherfucker, why don't you talk," and they started beating me, and I couldn't take it anymore, and I begged them to let me go. I said that I didn't know a thing, and they asked me who the commanders were, and I said that I didn't have the slightest idea, and they went on beating me. And a Mujahedin walked up to me behind my back and he grabbed me by the hair, and he put a knife to my neck and I felt that he would cut my skin, and I begged him and he let me go. And the other one who was translating, he said, "You Ustasha, why don't you talk? Now I'm going to blow your brains out," and he put a gun to my head, and I said "Please shoot, shoot." And he said, "Oh, no, no, you Ustasha motherfucker, you're not going to die that easy, no. Now you're going to see how you're going to get killed." And then (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he did, and he said, "Enough." And I turned to him all in blood, and (redacted) why did you do this to me? Why did you bring them here to kill me?" And he just waved his hand, and he walked out with the three Mujahedin. And I felt sick, I had a stomach ache, and I begged them to let me go to the toilet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, did they take something from you on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Everything, they took away everything, my watch, my ring, a memento I had from my late father, my jacket, my shoes, everything I had on me, everything. And I begged for them to let me go to the toilet, and they stared at me, and I was making signs that I had a stomach ache and could I get out, and they grabbed me by the hair and dragged me up the stairs. And I screamed because it was very painful, and the other one hit me on the head with a baton, and they dragged me by the hair outside. Then as I got outside, (redacted) was sitting out there on the grass and my mother-in-law, they were looking at me, and (redacted) and my mother-in-law were crying, and my mother-in-law said, "What did you do to my daughter-in-law?" And I went back to the basement. They took (redacted) and my mother-in-law back into the basement, and they locked me up in a different room which was some kind of a solitary cell, and I was there until the night. And I seemed to doze off, given all this torture, and I had dreamed that my throat was slit open.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That your throat was slit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that my throat was slit open and that I was bleeding, and I jumped up and I was banging at the door and hitting the walls. Everybody got up, they opened the door, and they said, "What is the matter with you? What are you doing?" And I said that my throat had been slit, and they took a torchlight and they took me to some kind of a mirror in the hallway, and they said, "See, your throat isn't slit. What are you saying?" And I begged them to bring my mother-in-law to stay with me, and they did bring her in to stay with me. The next day, we went to the basement again. They brought us dinner, lentils and some kind of horrible bread that you couldn't eat. And then they came and called out (redacted)'s name. They called him (redacted). From his young days, he was called (redacted). And then he went out, and then they asked him how old he was, et cetera, and then they said, "You were an Ustasha during the Second World War," and he said, "No, I was in the Partizans," and they said, "No, no, no, we know you, you Ustasha motherfucker, we know," and then they took him away and I never saw him again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you hear? Tell the Court what happened to the man born in 1929, (redacted)?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, from (redacted), you mean? Who do you mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm thinking of (redacted). What happened to him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, two or three days went by. They were all drunk. The Krajina men made some mistakes, and they turned us out of the room where I was, and that's where they locked them up, and we all went out into the sunlight for a bit because it was very cold. And I asked one of the men from Krajina, "Where is (redacted)? How come (redacted) isn't here?" And he said, "(redacted) has gone down there with the dead across the border. His son had the money to pay for him to be exchanged. Do you have any money so that you can be exchanged?" I said I had no money, and he said, "Well, then, you're going to have to rot here."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did (redacted) survive? What, in fact, happened to him? Explain to the Court.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he was taken to Mile, and they all demined the fields with our people. I was to go, but maybe somebody saved me from this. And then afterwards the Krajina people arrived.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before you go on to the next event with the Krajina men, what does it mean, "Take you to the mines," how did they use civilians such as (redacted) from your own village? Could you give us a detailed description of what you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What they would do is they would take somebody, a man, and they would let the man go in front of them to demine the field. And they took over a trench with (redacted), and they would allow these people to go in front of them, and that man would die, the mines would explode and then they would follow afterwards. Than is how they made this breakthrough across the minefields.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you wish to say that the Croats sent civilians to the minefield so that the, if the mines were exploded then the army would be able to pass?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. And when I cried and said, "I hope my son was not wounded," and he said, "Well, it would be better for him to be wounded, because had he not gone he would have gone up to the frontline, and that was what would happen".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There seems to be an error in the interpretation. I'm going to say what you said and you can either confirm that or deny it. The army of Bosnia-Herzegovina would send the Croat civilians out into the minefields ahead of them so as to activate the mines and clear the passage for them to pass?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, that is what I mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we're going to move on to an event, to the following event, when explosives were tied to your body. This was on the 10th day. Could you explain to the Trial Chamber what happened on the 10th day of your confinement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 10th day of my imprisonment, the Krajina men came and called me to come out. I went out, I was beaten up, completely, and they started interrogating me. I was not able to walk, and one of the Krajina men asked me, "What happened to you? Who beat you up?" And I said, "The Mujahedin," and he asked me, "Did they rape you?" And I said, "No." And he said, "You're very lucky, you're a lucky woman." And he said, "You're going to help us, you're going to help us save your son." And I said, "How?" "Well," he said, "you're going to go and take out our dead bodies from the no man's land in between the two zones." And I said, "I don't dare do that." And he said, "You want to save your child?" And I said, "Yes, I do." "Well," he said, "then you're going to do that".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one moment, please, the interim zone, could you explain to the Court what you mean by the "no man's land"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the land between the two borders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What two borders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The two borders, frontiers, between us and the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you want to say between the two frontlines; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, between the two frontlines. And they had started this breakthrough and encountered mines and died, and that is where their bodies remained. They were the men from Krajina. And so we wanted, they wanted me to bring out their dead, to pick up the dead bodies from this "no man's land". They came to collect me the next day, I didn't know it was as terrible as it was. I thought, I was happy because I thought I would be seeing my child. But they took me up there to a house, it belonged to (redacted), and they brought some mines and explosives, and they put me there and asked me, "Would it be difficult for you to carry this across, to go over there?" I was just numb and I cried, I looked at all this, and they took the mines and explosives and placed it on my body and put some sticky tape to attach the explosives to my body. And then a young man came up, one of the Krajina men, and he said, "Don't do that. I was with her son last night, I talked to him. Perhaps her son could do that instead of her. She won't succeed in doing this, but she will try."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he was thinking of your second son who was in the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. He asked about us, whether we were alive, and I told her son that yes, they were alive, and that the young son was in hospital, and I think that the son would do this for his mother. And then they took off the explosives and took me to where this young man had been speaking. They gave me a megaphone and said, "Call your son and ask him to do this job for you, if he has a mother." I called and called, but there was no answer from my son. It was only my neighbour who responded to my call. He asked me what I wanted, and I said, "There are some dead people here, some dead bodies, the Krajina men dead bodies, can you take the dead bodies out so I don't have to do it." He said, "That is impossible for you to do, we will do it. Wait for two or three hours until we do this, until we see, and we will say what we're able to do." And we waited there, and time passed. They gave me a loud speaker once again, a megaphone to call to them, and I called out to them and they said, "We found nobody, there is nobody there." And the person that wanted to find these other people was a relation of the men that were lying dead there, and he said, "Say that there is somebody, and if they want to do this job they can."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please try to avoid mentioning any names, we are going to delete them from the transcript, but please try not to mention your own name. So these two men made a decision, and what about the bodies on this, this "no man's land", were you able to take away the bodies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were, and they were exchanged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, when did your troubles and horrors come to an end? When were you released from the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 9th of November. And when this came about the Red Cross arrived and took an inventory of all of us and said we were now secure and safe and that nobody would harm us until the exchange took place. And I was exchanged on the 9th of November. The exchange team came to collect me and I was very happy. And I rushed out thinking that they were bringing me my child, but that was not the case. My child was not there. They exchanged me. And after the 24th my child came away, but it was not my child, it was just half my child, half my child.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "half your child," what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was just skin and bone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were exchanged on the 9th of November, 1993, would you remind the Court when you were arrested as a civilian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was arrested on the 18th of September, and on the 9th of November I left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After they let you depart from the camp, you lived in, you were housed in a building below which there was a mortuary.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see many funerals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, everybody passing by there. I saw all this with my own eyes. I saw them come to the hall, 32 from Krizancevo Selo. They were terrible massacres, they were all massacred, and I saw one boy, his feet were sticking up like this (indicating) and he had no meat on the feet, on his feet, just bones.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We're now going to look at a videotape which I should like to ask you to look at carefully, and perhaps later on we shall have some questions to ask you. So may we have the lights dimmed, please, and see the videotape until the end. There are three sequences. (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the scene from the mortuary in Vitez? Can you see properly? Something seems to have been blocked.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: May we wind it back to the beginning, please? Let's have the tape from the beginning. And if there is any sound, may we have the sound track, too? But please wind it back to the beginning, and put up the volume.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was night time, and all of them were buried during the night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These are people in front of the mortuary, are they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they are. These are people standing in front of the mortuary. It wasn't a mortuary, it was just an unfinished building, a makeshift mortuary, no doors, nothing. That's where they took the dead bodies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were scenes of this kind frequently seen in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, very frequently. They were daily, practically daily occurrences.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, were there mass funerals attended by lots of people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were, they were mass funerals attended by a great many people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise this man?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, his wife and son died. This woman's husband was killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, please, from Krizancevo Selo, how many bodies were brought here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first time 32 bodies were brought, the ones I saw, 32 bodies, on the first occasion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know from Bobasi how many bodies were brought?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I was in prison up there when the bodies from Bobasi were brought. I only know from Krizancevo Selo and Buhine Kuce.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about Buhine Kuce, how many bodies from there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, please, while we're looking at this, your village, you said that there were 50 Croat houses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any house remain standing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not a single house remained standing. Everything had been destroyed and burned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, please, during these funerals, by force of circumstance you lived in the environs, these are mass funerals, did you encounter women from Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was among them. They were embittered, they were bitter, they cursed and swore.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did they curse and swear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They cursed Cerkez and Blaskic. They cursed them and said that it was their fault that all this had happened because they had protected the Muslims and that our people had died, and they were bitter. And on that occasion they might have -- had they met any one of these on this occasion they wouldn't have fared well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they were bitter with Cerkez, the commander of the Vitez Brigade, and Blaskic, as well, the commander, for protecting the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Give us an example, for example, what did the women at the funeral mention, as an example? How did Blaskic and Cerkez protect these people? What did they not allow to take place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, no attacks, particularly on old Vitez, Stari Vitez, because snipers kept hitting Stari Vitez and people died every day, sometimes, on some days five people would die. Darko Kraljevic organised an attack, and he thought that they would help him with their guns. But there was no command to help the people, and 21 people died on the occasion, and they all cursed them and swore them, and said, "Well, God if we could just get hold of them, we know what we would do to them".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think there has been an error in the transcript. So the snipers did not shoot at Stari Vitez but from Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, they were shooting from Stari Vitez, at us, from snipers, and somebody was always killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was in Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the Muslims in Stari Vitez. And there was to have been an attack, because it was the central part of Vitez there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the Croats, for the most part, lived in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, whereas in Stari Vitez, in the middle of town, this is where the Muslims lived. And everybody from around shot at us, from all around. And there was to be an operation launched there when Darko Kraljevic led that operation and asked the commanders, asked Cerkez and Blaskic to help him with the gunnery; but they would not allow this. And that is where 21 men died.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Croats, you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, please, what did you hear these women saying? Why did Blaskic and Cerkez not allow the artillery to attack Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they said, what about the population, the population was not able to escape, and what would happen to the population, it would be a sort of massacre, I don't know. So that they protected them. Whereas, our folk died.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "protected them," you mean they protected the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, the Muslims, they protected the Muslims, and in that respect, they really were protected by them. And our people, the people of Vitez, were bitter about this, and they will never forgive them for that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We would like to offer the tape into evidence, or first the map, D460, under seal. Also, we offer the tape, it will be D461, so this will be a Defence Exhibit. Mr. President, we have concluded the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No objection from the Prosecutor as regarding the tendering of those exhibits?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I would like a clarification here. There were two films that were shown, there were two cassettes; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: One.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: No? Then D461A concerns the hospital, and B is the film we have just seen, but it is the same tape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No comments from the Prosecutor? Mr. Cayley? In light of what was just said, questions and answers, do you feel that you are in a position -- I know you're capable of doing it, but are you in a position to conduct your cross-examination, or would you like some time? What's your opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The position that we take, Mr. President, is the witness should come back tomorrow. It may well be that after I've considered matters I don't have any questions, but at the moment I'm not in a position to say whether I do or not. There are some other comments I would actually also like to make about the summary in respect of this witness, but I think that should be done outside the presence of the witness, because I don't wish to, in any way, give the impression to the witness that we minimise her suffering. So if that could be done with the witness outside the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Let me first explain to the witness what is happening. Witness DQ, there was a mistake in the spelling of your first name, and that did not allow the opposing party, that is the Office of the Prosecutor, to prepare properly and equitably so that the cross-examination could be conducted. That's why we're going to ask you to come back tomorrow. I would like you to remain in The Hague a little bit longer, but that's for the sake of equitable justice. The Judges are here to be sure both parties have the time to say what they need to say. It's unfortunate, but that's how things are. You will be taken care of by the Victims and Witnesses Unit, and you will stay in The Hague a little bit longer. We're going to ask you to withdraw, because I believe the Prosecutor has a statement he wishes to make, or rather a comment. We thank you for having come today, and we will see you tomorrow at 10.00 in the morning. And in the meantime, try to rest.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We're going to lower the curtain so you can leave the courtroom without anybody being able to see your face. All right, you can now stand and we could say good-bye to you until tomorrow morning. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley, you had a comment you wanted to make? This is a public hearing, is it not? Yes, it is, but if this doesn't affect the witness's protective measures we can remain in public.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think it would be prudent, Mr. President, to actually move into a private session while we're discussing this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well, let's move into a private session. (Private session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. The Court stands adjourned and we will resume at 2.30. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.44 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Open session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We can now resume. Have the accused brought in, please. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Is this a protected witness, Mr. Nobilo?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, he is, Mr. President, a protected witness. Pseudonym and face distortion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Registrar, have the witness brought in. What is the pseudonym? What will this be, DR? (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Do you hear me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I'm the Presiding Judge. Don't be afraid of anything, you are before Judges. We are not wearing our robes, our Judges robes, but I can assure you we are Judges. Do not be afraid --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not afraid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: First of all, we're going to ask you to stand and to look at your name -- what are we going to do, Mr. Registrar? We're going to ask you to read your name but not to state your name. Don't say it. Can you see? Is that, in fact, your name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Okay. We're going to ask you to remain standing a little while longer, because we're going to ask you to take a solemn declaration. The registrar is going to read you a statement, and then you repeat after him what he says. All right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right, Witness DR. We're going to call you DR in order to protect you. You may be seated now. This means that your face does not show on the screen and we're going to use two letters to refer to you. Be careful when you answer the questions. Do not give out any information which might identify you. If that should happen, do not worry. There are ways that we can erase from the transcript what you may have said that might identify you. First, you will be asked questions by the attorney who asked you to come. That is Mr. Nobilo. Let me remind you that the accused is in this courtroom, to your left; that is General Blaskic. Speak without fear, without hatred. Try to tell us what you have to say. We have a summary of your testimony that has to do with attacks against certain villages, and you can say what you experienced, but first you're going to answer Mr. Nobilo's questions. Mr. Nobilo, proceed, please. Examined by Mr. Nobilo:

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I would like to ask for a private session for one or two minutes for identification purposes, and to hand out a map, because the map shows the position and locality of the village from which the protected witness comes. (Private session)

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: (Open session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Nobilo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your village, the village you lived in, what were the relationships between the Croats and Muslims before all these hostilities started?

utterances.speaker: DR
utterances.text: They were fine relations. We didn't differ much in anything. When my sons went in the army, they would come to visit us. If we had any roast being prepared, roast meat being prepared, then we would -- they would come and we were all together, all sat down together, and they were good neighbourly relations. Nobody would depart and saying anything ill to anybody. We all lived together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could I ask you to slow down, please? I'm going to ask you something now, for this to be made clear to the -- I'm going to ask you something for clarification purposes. When you say "they" would come, who did you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: DR
utterances.text: I'm thinking of the Muslims. We were all together. We were just separated by a road, and the Muslims, our neighbours, would come visiting, and we would go visiting, we would visit them, I went with my husband, when one of their children would go to the army. We had a nice time. They would always give us some nice refreshments. And they would come to our house too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. When you told the Court that the Muslims would come visiting and you would slaughter a sheep for them, why did you do that?

utterances.speaker: DR
utterances.text: Well, we did that because we respected them. There was no hatred between us, and we -- they had lunch at my place, and we prepared this sheep, and a year ago we had no problems, no changes. We didn't know that any -- there would be ever any troubles between us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you wish to say that out of respect towards the Muslim traditions, you gave them meat from a sheep and not from pigs?

utterances.speaker: DR
utterances.text: Yes. They had their own table, their own things to eat, what they wanted to drink, if they wanted any alcoholic beverage, if they did not, they would be given fruit juices. So we always took this into account, and gave them the mutton and sheep to eat so that we would never give any other meat to them, we wouldn't be underhanded in that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one moment, please. Let me ask you my question. I asked you whether you slaughtered the sheep to give them sheep instead of pork and so respect their customs, the Muslim customs?

utterances.speaker: DR
utterances.text: Yes, that's quite right. We would slaughter a sheep for them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, tell me please, before the 8th of June, 1993, when the conflict broke out and your village was attacked, what were the first misunderstandings between the Muslims and Croats, particularly the younger people who had weapons?

utterances.speaker: DR
utterances.text: Well, they had weapons, but nobody had a great deal, perhaps one rifle or two rifles, depending. And the misunderstanding broke out in the following way: They wanted, the Muslims wanted to have the main command at Naodici, which is where the Mujahedin were. We all knew that. They lived there. They had been living there for more than a year. And they wanted the command headquarters to be at Naodici. That's what the Muslims wanted. Our people didn't agree with that, and that's where the first misunderstandings broke out between our men and the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you went to Mehurici, to the market, did you see the Mujahedin? If so, describe what they looked like.

utterances.speaker: DR
utterances.text: Yes, we did see the Mujahedin. They came-- they are different from our people. They wore different clothing. They had long robes and they had something white over their heads and long beards, and they were rather strange, stranger than our own folk. Sometimes we would go to market and see them and we wondered what they were doing here, because there were more and more of them every day. That's what it was like. And it wasn't -- you see, they would turn up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, the local Muslims, both men and women, before this war did they differ essentially in the way they dressed from the local Croats?

utterances.speaker: DR
utterances.text: Well, they started to. Young women wore the same things as us Croats, but afterwards they began wearing the Turkish striped chalvara trousers. So they didn't differ to begin with, but later on they began covering themselves up, and I don't remember them having been covered up before, but our grandmothers used to tell us that they once dressed like that, but that is over 50 years ago, but suddenly they began covering themselves up. Then we began to panic somewhat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say that the women began covering themselves up, would you describe to the Court what you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: DR
utterances.text: Well, they would wear a long black dress and above here there would be a black scarf, and they would cover their faces, and here they would just have a little sort of -- you could see their eyes a little bit but everything would be covered. How shall I put it? You know, it was slightly transparent so they could see a little bit. But this -- we found this very strange when we started seeing people dressed in this way, our neighbours dressed in this way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this wasn't the custom previously?

utterances.speaker: DR
utterances.text: No, it never existed. It wasn't the custom. I never had occasion to see that type of dress, and of course, the younger people never saw anything of that kind before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Amongst the people in buses and the men between, the discussions between the Muslim men and Croat men, what led to dissension?

utterances.speaker: DR
utterances.text: I don't know, it was a long time ago when they ruled Bosnia and they said that ours used to marry, and they always spent the first night with our bride, and then he said in one of the buses on one occasion, the same times here with us again today, and that was the source of discontent. It's the time when we are sleeping with your women again. And this led to a great deal of panic and a lot of excitement, and brawls broke out. And so that was what was amiss. It was an insult for our men. But that's what the older folk used to tell us about this, but none of the younger people remembered any of this happening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So are you, in fact, referring to the right of the Bays, the Turkish Bays to sleep with young Christian brides and have to spend their first night with the Bays?

utterances.speaker: DR
utterances.text: This was the custom, yes, this was the old custom. There were stories handed down from our forefathers that things like this used to happen in Turkish times. But with the present generations, none of us ever experienced that. And people panicked, why these stories should be brought up again, and there was not the confidence and trust that there was between the two people previously.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let's move towards events in your village, the events that began on the 8th of June 1993. But before we do that, were there any incidents that broke out with regard to the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: DR
utterances.text: Well, they were not together, but they went up to the frontlines, the area called Skulje towards the Chetniks. The Muslims went and our own men went, ours had their own buses, and the Muslims had their own buses. And my son was amongst them. And when the first incident broke out, they were met at Zukica bridge, three days prior to that particular unfortunate day which hit us all so bad. They stood in front of the bus, it was a truck, I don't remember whether it was a truck covered with a canvas or a bus or whatever, because this was further off from our village, I'm not quite sure, but they met this truck or vehicle or bus, whatever it was, there were 25 of our young men in it, and they took away their rifles, and disarmed them and provoked them. Then our army was up there at Ovnak, and they took our men prisoners and took some of their prisoners. Then there was an agreement, and there were negotiations, at Ovnak, and then they let our men go but they took away their ammunition, they returned their rifles and they would release the other people, and that is how that incident took place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For purposes of the transcript, when you say ours, you were are referring to the Croats, and when you say theirs, you're thinking about the Muslims; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DR
utterances.text: Yes, the Muslims, yes. Yes, they were Muslims, and so they returned their rifles but kept the ammunition, they took all their ammunition away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One day prior to the attack what the Muslims do to the shepherds and sheep, Croat shepherds and their sheep?

utterances.speaker: DR
utterances.text: Prior to the attack they went up there and our shepherds could not go to our mountain, and they say that the Muslim army had gone out onto our side, that was Gorcevica and Vlasic mountain, and our shepherds had gone to Mount Vlasic. And then one day prior to the attack, it was the 7th and the attack was on the 8th, they took prisoner from my own village, one of my neighbours, my husband's -- her sheep, she had 200 sheep and the other one had 300 sheep, and the daughter-in-law was there with her small children, she had three children, the eldest child was 6 years old. So we heard in the evening that (redacted) was taken prisoner, that all his sheep had been confiscated and he was at Meuric, and it was very late, there was a great deal of panic all over the place during that night, and in the morning we were attacked and that was what happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say the 7th and then you say the 8th, are you speaking of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: DR
utterances.text: Yes, yes, on the 7th --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What month?

utterances.speaker: DR
utterances.text: It was June, it was the 7th day of June when the sheep were taken away and the shepherds turned away. There were two from our village and perhaps more from other villages, but I know exactly who was taken from my own village, but there were others taken away as well. There were a lot of these shepherds and they were taken to Meuric. And (redacted), I know they beat him up and he died quite recently. They beat up his children, they broke his children's teeth, and that's what happened. I know for a fact that happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you were afraid. On the night before the attack, did you spend the night in your village or did you go somewhere else to spend the night? That is to say, the civilians from your village.

utterances.speaker: DR
utterances.text: When the weapons were taken away from our men, our soldiers, when their weapons were taken away, down there at (redacted) bridge, women and children weren't there, and they went into the village I was born in, there aren't any Muslims living there, and I stayed with my husband at home, and my children were there, too. So we were there at home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the civilians?

utterances.speaker: DR
utterances.text: The civilians, my eight young grandchildren, my daughters-in-law, everybody, they spent the night down there. I mean, everybody wanted to be safe. I mean, everybody, you know, the Croat population, they wanted to be safe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you say "down there," what do you mean by "down there"?

utterances.speaker: DR
utterances.text: Down there is (redacted). That's where I was born. (redacted) and (redacted). (redacted) we lived with the Muslims, and down in (redacted) there were no Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you and your husband remained in your village in (redacted). And what happened at dawn, at 3.30 a.m., on the 8th of June, 1993? Could you describe this for the Trial Chamber, please?

utterances.speaker: DR
utterances.text: Well, they, the menfolk and the child came at dawn, he went to sleep for a little while, and (redacted), a village across the road from our own village and house, and around 3.30 a.m., we saw the shelling of that village and we saw it on fire. Mortars fell and the houses were set on fire, and we wondered who was doing this shooting, and we had absolutely no idea what was happening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is (redacted) a Croat village?

utterances.speaker: DR
utterances.text: Yes, (redacted) and (redacted) and these are all Croat villages. And that's, we were very disturbed, and I went in to wake up my youngest son, and I said to my son, "There's shooting, get up, a shell might fall, a mortar might fall on our house." And I had two other sons, they had houses up above my own house, and they were up there, just divided by a road from the Muslims. And they were encircled, they were surrounded, and the shooting started, and shooting started at my house, and they were shooting at my husband and myself and my children, and fire broke out all over the place. And one of his, Ahmic arrived, he said, "You should flee with them, escape with them, and I will stay with the children." And that's what happened. He opened a door below my house, you see, you have to pass this little gate, there's a sort of gate below the house, and I went with my relation and his uncle and we escaped towards (redacted), that is what it was called, and all our people escaped along this route. They stayed behind me. I went up, emerged from the top, the army brought out my mother-in-law. In at the top part of our village, those were Croat houses up there, and I found my mother-in-law there and two other women. I looked for my husband, my mother-in-law could not escape and I couldn't carry her. At that moment my children arrived, and they said, "(redacted) has died," they called him by his name, they said, "(redacted) has died" and I lost control.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean the father?

utterances.speaker: DR
utterances.text: Yes. And they did not dare tell my mother-in-law.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, how old was your mother-in-law?

utterances.speaker: DR
utterances.text: She was born in 1912, and we didn't dare tell her that her son had been killed, so I said, "Children, you run off, you escape," but I couldn't leave my mother-in-law. I lived with her for a long time, she had nobody else, she had my husband and she had a daughter, and we will be living together for 36 years and I didn't have the heart to leave her there. So I told my children to flee for their lives, but that I would stay with my mother-in-law, and if they killed me what could I do. I wanted to stay with her. I couldn't leave her. So my eldest son was very close to me and he liked his grandmother very much and he kept turning back to see what we were doing, and he would go off and then return. And he said, "Don't stay there, don't stay in the house, let me, let us carry the grandmother up to some rocks which would provide shelter" and he took up his grandmother and managed to carry her away. But it began raining, and we were able to take shelter in a cave, it was a kind of a cave, and then they went towards (redacted). And a little time after that, these two, the two boys returned. And I said, "Why have you come back?" And they said, "Well, we have been blocked, because the army is coming from up there, and we have been surrounded, and we can't go anywhere anymore."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you found yourself -- were you in the forest, in the mountain above your village, in the vicinity of your village?

utterances.speaker: DR
utterances.text: Yes, close to my village. We could see each of our houses because we were up above the village, and so we could see our houses down below.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What could you see from this shelter you had taken in the forest and on the hill?

utterances.speaker: DR
utterances.text: I could see everything. I saw my husband dead, I saw my house as if it was in the palm of my hand. And when the army started coming, then they began to celebrate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which army?

utterances.speaker: DR
utterances.text: The Muslim army, we were all expelled and it was very easy to expel us, in fact, the people withdrew. They started fleeing, they had no weapons, and they said there are thousands of them coming over, this Muslim army is coming upon us. And we stayed up there on this hillside, and they said were it not for the shelling -- what was I saying?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've forgotten. Tell us, you're in the wood and up on the mountainside, and you're looking down onto the village. Tell us, what did you see happening in the village? What were your neighbours and the Muslim army doing?

utterances.speaker: DR
utterances.text: The army had taken the best house. This man worked abroad and he had the best house in the village, and they burned down the -- they burned the house, it was the best house in the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you turn to the Judges, please?

utterances.speaker: DR
utterances.text: And one of them had a harmonica and he played the harmonica and they played and danced, it was sort of a celebration for having expelled us. And we could see all this from our vantage point, from where we were in the forest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What else did you see? Were other houses burning? Was there looting?

utterances.speaker: DR
