utterances.text: Well, they then said they came to the conclusion that they were not allowed to burn the houses because the Croats were rich, but the best thing was to loot the house, and then once you have looted the houses you can set fire to them. Then they went about the village looting, pilfering whatever they could find.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of things did they take from the houses?

utterances.speaker: DR
utterances.text: They took out furniture, they took food, they took everything away, whatever they came across, whatever they found, gold, money. I left my house without anything on my back. I took nothing from my house at all, just the clothes that I was wearing, and everything was left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the livestock? Did they take the livestock away?

utterances.speaker: DR
utterances.text: What do you mean? Oh, yes, livestock, cows and everything, yes they would take cows, slaughter the pigs. They took two men prisoner, two of our men, two Croats, and they dug the pigs and divided the cows up and went towards (redacted), and that's what it was like.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when they had looted the village, did they set fire to the houses?

utterances.speaker: DR
utterances.text: Yes, everything was set fire to. Of my three houses, I only have one house left which is inhabited by the locals, but I have nothing any more, nobody living there, and nobody can live there, they have nowhere to go back to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From the place where you stood, did you see the largest Croat village there, Grahovcici?

utterances.speaker: DR
utterances.text: Yes, then we went to the woods, we wanted to move to (redacted). Night fell while we were in the woods, and we saw Grahovcici on fire. The cows were making a terrible noise, all the people had fled, some of the cows were still in the barn. That is what we saw during the night. Then, when it dawned, it was the 8th before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it was the 9th?

utterances.speaker: DR
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So was that the 9th of June?

utterances.speaker: DR
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. And then we withdrew into the forest, we had no place to run. So what was I saying? Then we went to the woods. And (redacted) found us. He came to see his wife, to look for his wife, and then he saw us, and he said, "Let's go home." And he said, "My goodness I had such good neighbours, nobody would kill me." And (redacted) said to him, "(redacted) I don't dare go, I don't dare leave this place until something happens. I don't know, there is panic in the village, the army is out there." So we were there in the woods. Then my sons, my two sons, too, and then there was a Croat house that stood out there without any houses around it, and then we went to see whether there was some food over there, because we hadn't had anything to eat, we were all wet, we got caught in the rain. Two of my sons went there and found a loaf of bread that was packed. The people had obviously wanted to take it, but they didn't have time to take it; so my two sons brought it to us, and they brought us some cheese and they brought us a few eggs, and we had a bite to eat. (redacted) stayed there, and then we spent the night there again, until the 10th of June. Well, after daybreak on Thursday, my children were there when (redacted) went to have a drink of water, but he stood on a mine and his foot was blown up. And some shepherds saw him, and I said, "I want to surrender." And I said, "Children, you surrender, too, you have not deserved to die at the hand of your neighbours. I imagine they will take you to the penitentiary in Zenica."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the prison?

utterances.speaker: DR
utterances.text: Yes, yes, the prison, the penitentiary down there. And my children stayed on with (redacted) and I went to the village. And they treated us as if we had carried some big guns, they wanted to kill us off. And they hit (redacted) with a rifle butt here, and then they hit me on the head, and they broke my arm, and I was a bit dizzy. And they said, "Come with us and tell us where your positions are." And they were saying that they could have killed all of us up there. When I went up there with

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: DR
utterances.text: He grabbed my son by the hair and he started hitting him. And I said, "Are you his colleague from work?" And he said, "Yes, I used to be, but I'm not anymore, and now I am going to have a showdown with him." And I said, "My goodness, today he was saying that he would like to find one of his colleagues from work in order to surrender to him." So he let him go, he didn't beat him anymore, and he was crying and said, "(redacted) is dead." And this guy came and said that he would kill my son, and this other soldier jumped up and said, "No, no, no, you're not supposed to kill him," and they said, "what do we know?" And then they panicked, and he had to bring him under pressure, and when they brought him in his head was broken up here with a knife.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you talking about one of your sons, his head was broken?

utterances.speaker: DR
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's what I'm saying. And they untied their hands, both of them, and they said one of them should carry his grandmother and the other one should carry (redacted). And this one soldier said that they should put (redacted) down. Then he said that we should turn our heads away and we turned our heads and they killed him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say (redacted), that is the man who was wounded?

utterances.speaker: DR
utterances.text: Yes, yes, the (redacted) whose wife was with us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he was wounded because he stepped on a mine, right, is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: DR
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's what I'm saying. And we went to the village to take him to Zenica so he would be helped there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me, could we slow down a bit? We're talking too fast. When I put a question to you, could you please wait for a while, for me to finish the question, because I'm speaking slowly on purpose so the interpreters would have enough time to interpret everything that you're saying.

utterances.speaker: DR
utterances.text: Yes, but I get carried away, you know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You know, it's these people who talk that you hear through the headphones, but just try to relax and we will continue slowly. Please don't concentrate on what you hear here in your headphones, concentrate on my questions. So now I'm going to put some questions to you. At that point in time, you had two of your sons with you. Do not mention their names. Two of your sons were with you. Where was your third son?

utterances.speaker: DR
utterances.text: I don't understand this. This is some kind of foreign talk.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The channel has changed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. We're going fix that for you.

utterances.speaker: DR
utterances.text: I hear this foreign talk and it bothers me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Do you hear me?

utterances.speaker: DR
utterances.text: Yes, I do, all of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: When you answer, look at the Judges, please. Try to relax, take your time when you answer.

utterances.speaker: DR
utterances.text: Fine. Fine. This really bothered me so -- I'm terribly sorry. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: But you can speak; right? You know how to speak. Okay. Get your wits together and in a little while we'll take a pause.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, when you're fumbling with the buttons in front of you, then you get this foreign language into your headphones because you change these buttons in front of you. So if it happens again, just tell us and we'll help you. All right. So you were in captivity and two of your sons were in captivity, and they killed this wounded man and you weren't supposed to watch.

utterances.speaker: DR
utterances.text: No, no, no. We could not watch.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And there was shooting all over?

utterances.speaker: DR
utterances.text: No, no, no, we didn't dare look. No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, could you calmly tell us about what happen to your sons right in front of you, those who were taken prisoner by the BH army? Explain that to us, please.

utterances.speaker: DR
utterances.text: Well, they separated them from us immediately. They put us into a house that used to be a Croat house, and I found, over there, some of our other villagers who could not run away, and my children were separated from me. It was already night time by then, and they took them to a Muslim village, and they beat them black and blue, as we would say, black and blue. Then I found these people from my village, (redacted) and his wife (redacted), and (redacted), and (redacted).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And (redacted)?

utterances.speaker: DR
utterances.text: Yes, yes. (redacted) was there too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, were these people old and disabled?

utterances.speaker: DR
utterances.text: Yes. All of them old people who could not run, who had pain in their legs, and they couldn't run away with the other people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened after that?

utterances.speaker: DR
utterances.text: I found (redacted), who was beaten up there, and his ribs were broken. (redacted) came. I mean, he had a shop, and he knew that he would have money on him, he provoked him and said all sorts of things to him, and he hid this money into his cap.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you referring to (redacted)?

utterances.speaker: DR
utterances.text: Yes, I'm referring to (redacted). And he had 2.800; that's what he said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Two thousand eight hundred of what?

utterances.speaker: DR
utterances.text: Of money. I mean, (redacted). So he took it all with him. He said that he would go and bring the Mujahedin to slaughter him. Then this other one jumped out of the window. He couldn't really jump that far, so his collar bone broke and also his ribs were broken. I found him there in the house all broken up like that. Then when night fell, then they took us down there to their village, their Muslim village, towards a house. Then my children came, and they had to carry their grandmother again. Then we came to a garage, and then they lined us up in front of the garage and they said, "Why don't you all hold hands now and we're going to execute all of you."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they used weapons?

utterances.speaker: DR
utterances.text: Yes, they used weapons. And we realised what our fate was. And it's not that I felt sorry -- I mean, I was there with my two sons, and if they were going to get killed, and then I thought, "Well, whatever." I mean, my husband had been killed too, so what good was it for me to go on living? So they opened this garage and we walked into the garage, and there was some kind of fuel in the garage. It was suffocating. It was awful. And -- and we actually spent the night there. They closed the door and they kept us there. The next day, at around 10.00 or 11.00 they opened up a bit, and we one by one we started getting out, and we said we were feeling sick, all of us. And we were all getting out, and there was a bit of water there and we managed to wash our faces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did they say they would do to you?

utterances.speaker: DR
utterances.text: Well, they said that -- they were saying that they wanted to kill us. And when I went out to get some water, I heard one of the soldiers saying that they would kill us, but I didn't say anything. One of them said that he would save us. And then it was Friday and the Muslims came to this mosque of theirs there. And then they were there at the mosque, and they would not spare them their lives. And then their colleague of his from work came, this was 5.00 in the evening, and he told my son to get up, and he said, "Get up," and then they both got up, and then I said, "Now what?" And he closed the door, and then this woman was out there, (redacted), and this (redacted), this colleague of my son's from work, he said "No, I don't want to kill this one." Then this other one, they took him away and they didn't let him go across the wall, they took him to the garden and then they killed him out there. Then I heard this rifle shot but we couldn't move, we couldn't do a thing. Then a taxi came. "Where are these two?" And they said, "No, no one's there." Then when I got out a soldier was carrying a pair of boots, and he was saying his -- his feet are going to get warm now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So did they kill the other son?

utterances.speaker: DR
utterances.text: Yes, yes. This other one, (redacted), yes, killed him too, yes. He said, "He can keep his feet warm tonight, his pig feet warm tonight." And they brought this Kombi, and they had these green bands on their heads, and they said, "Get in to the Kombi," and we got into the Kombi, and they said that they would kill everybody up there. Then they were talking about it all the time, how they would kill all of us, and they said, "No, we're not going to use any bullets. Why would we waste bullets on them?" And this Muslim who represented the civilian defence, he stood in front of the Kombi and said, "No, you're not going to kill all of them." Then he said, "Okay, come on out and move towards Susanj." And, "They're more your folks down there." Then we went down there and then --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a minute, please. Before we reach Susanj, could we just stop for a moment? Your two sons practically were killed in front of the garage where you were; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now I'm going to read out to you a list of persons from your village, and I'm going to ask you what happened to these people. Listen to me carefully. Do not say, "This is my son," or, "This is my husband," or whatever. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 17 (redacted). 18 All of these men and women, what happened to them?

utterances.speaker: DR
utterances.text: All of them were killed, all of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your village?

utterances.speaker: DR
utterances.text: Yes, all of them were killed. All of them were my neighbours. I knew all of them. All of them were killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And now tell us, you came to the village of Susanj. What happened to those old disabled people who you had already mentioned when you spoke before? What did you see there?

utterances.speaker: DR
utterances.text: When we entered the house we came upon crying, and they were all executed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many coffins did you see?

utterances.speaker: DR
utterances.text: There were about 19 coffins. On the next day it was a Saturday and that was when the funeral took place, and I attended the funeral. My son was there. He had died too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the third son -- your third son had died as well, was killed as well?

utterances.speaker: DR
utterances.text: Yes. But this one died in the fighting as opposed to the other two sons. Yes, that's right. And he found himself there. That was where he was, and that was where he was buried. And they came from Zenica, the people, and that was how it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the village of Susanj in the Zenica municipality, you spent some time in the village of Stranjane?

utterances.speaker: DR
utterances.text: We spent ten days there in Susanj, and after the funeral we went back, but we were not able to stay, we couldn't sleep the whole night, and they said that we ought to be slaughtered, and that we were their biggest target, and that is when I withdrew and I went to Stranjane that with my mother-in-law. I went to stay with a friend.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Stranjane was there looting going on there?

utterances.speaker: DR
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. When I got there, for a time there wasn't, but then incidents broke out there as well. And as they had looted everything that existed down below, then they did the same there. If anybody had a cow -- they would come in the evening and wanted to throw a bomb amongst children -- and they said, "Give us your cow." "We're going to kill your children with a bomb." (redacted)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in these events you lost your husband and three sons?

utterances.speaker: DR
utterances.text: Yes. In those events I lost my husband and three sons, and my mother-in-law died as well. A soldier hit her here with his boot, he kicked her in the back. She was an old woman and a very slight woman, and she died from the result of that kick a month and a half later. She had five daughters, and I lost my husband and my children.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the property you had, your house and the tractors and the farming machinery that you had, what happened?

utterances.speaker: DR
utterances.text: Well, just -- just the walls remain standing. Everything else has been looted. There's nothing else there. There's nowhere for me to go back, just the walls. Sometimes they even place an explosive under houses. So I haven't got anywhere to go back to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of the 5.000 or 6.000 Croats who lived in your parish, how many Croats live there today?

utterances.speaker: DR
utterances.text: There's not a single one. How can they live? Because this was the largest Croatian village, now there is nobody left. In Miletici there is nobody left. In Orahovice there is nobody. Now in Brajkovici, the priest returned to Brajkovici and perhaps three or four other individuals, but otherwise, there's nobody there any more. Of the 5.000 or 6.000 that used to live there, we've all gone away from there or been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: That is all, Mr. President. We have completed our examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: What number does the map have?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It's D462, and it's a confidential exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe? Witness DR, we're now going to give the floor to the representative from the Office of the Prosecutor. That's the procedure in a court. Cross-examined by Mr. Kehoe:

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I'll be very brief. It's not just going to be -- I would like to ask a question about the municipality. Counsel, should we go into private session on that? I look for guidance from you on that issue. To talk about the witness's municipality without mentioning the village. I will be guided by your instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: If I have understood you correctly, we're going to speak about the municipality where the village was located. Well then, that's not necessary because it's a small village in a big municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. There's your answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's fine. My concern was in the spirit of caution. I just thought I'd raise that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I may, witness, DR, my name is Greg Kehoe. I work for the office of the Prosecutor. My two colleagues, to my immediate right is Mr. Harmon, and to his right is Mr. Andrew Cayley. Witness DR, what municipality was your village in?

utterances.speaker: DR
utterances.text: Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would it --

utterances.speaker: DR
utterances.text: It belonged to Travnik. It was the municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would it be fair to say, without mentioning the name of your village, please, that it was relatively close to the Zenica municipality; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DR
utterances.text: Well, Travnik and Zenica, they weren't that near or that far away, actually, by bus. I don't know the exact number of kilometres, I never counted them. Zenica was another municipality and Travnik was a separate municipality. I was from the municipality of Travnik myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness DR, you talked to us about your life in your village, the camaraderie and the spirit of co-existence you had with your Bosnian Muslim neighbours and how you celebrated together on occasions such as sending your respective sons off to the JNA. Now, Witness DR, did that spirit of camaraderie continue for quite some time prior to these events on the 8th of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: DR
utterances.text: Well, it continued up until the year when the war broke out and what have you else, everything that took place afterwards. Let me tell you one thing quite clearly and honestly; the elections, as soon as the elections were held there was some distrust between ourselves and the Muslims, and as they were close to me, they always thought about the fact that Bosnia would belong to them and that there wouldn't be any more of us, and this mistrust began to fester and we were not as close as we had formerly been.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness DR, there were no attacks on your village prior to the 8th of June, 1993; were there?

utterances.speaker: DR
utterances.text: No, no attacks of any kind. There was nothing before that. They were in their village, the Muslims were in their village, and our own people the Croats were in our village, but they would talk together or they would talk to one another and so on, but there were no attacks, there was nothing before that. We were surprised by it. I didn't think they would kill my children, because we were not on bad terms. I don't know what happened. I have actually no idea what happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And until that time, just taking your words, Witness DR, you were on good terms with your Muslim neighbours until the 8th of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: DR
utterances.text: Yes. We were not on bad terms, as I say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, in fact, Witness DR, at least some of your neighbours, your Muslim neighbours helped you during this very, very trying incident; didn't they?

utterances.speaker: DR
utterances.text: Nobody wanted to help us at all. I cried out when they arrested my children and when they -- when I saw that they were going to kill them. I said, "Is there anybody older here? Let them go to the army with you, but just leave them, let them live. Leave them alive," but nobody wanted to help.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, let me just go into private session for a moment and mention a name. I think it would probably be the safer course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead. (Private session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
